title: Indian-Origin Founders Built $560 Billion of Unicorn Value Abroad, Report Finds
excerpt: The Prosus-Dealroom Indian Diaspora Index found 205 overseas unicorns with at least one founder who grew up in India — worth more than the $349 billion attributed to 102 India-based unicorns.
body:
• 205 current and former unicorns outside India have at least one founder who grew up in India, worth $560 billion on a founder-share basis, according to the new Prosus-Dealroom Indian Diaspora Index.
  • 70 of those unicorns were built entirely by Indian-origin founding teams — including Zscaler, Rubrik and Nutanix — accounting for $243 billion.
  • 91% of the overseas cohort, or 187 companies, are based in the United States.
  • By comparison, 102 unicorns based in India account for $349 billion, led by Flipkart, Zomato and Groww.

Indian founders have built more unicorn value abroad than at home. Founders who grew up in India account for $560 billion of founder-share-attributed company value across 205 current and former unicorns outside the country, according to the Indian Diaspora Index, a new report by Prosus and Dealroom — comfortably ahead of the $349 billion attributed to the founders of 102 India-based unicorns.

The index tracked every overseas unicorn with at least one founder who grew up in India, and the headline finding is stark: India's entrepreneurial talent is creating the bulk of its billion-dollar value outside India's borders.

"Founders who grew up in India account for USD 560 billion of founder-share-attributed company value in current and former unicorns abroad."

— Prosus-Dealroom Indian Diaspora Index

Two cohorts, one pattern

The $560 billion splits into two distinct groups. Seventy unicorns worth a combined $243 billion were built entirely by Indian-origin founding teams — among them Zscaler, founded by Jay Chaudhry; Rubrik, founded by Bipul Sinha, Arvind Jain, Arvind Nithrakashyap and Soham Mazumdar; Nutanix, founded by Dheeraj Pandey, Ajeet Singh and Mohit Aron; and Skild, founded by Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta.

The other 135 unicorns, contributing $317 billion on a founder-share basis, were built by mixed founding teams with Indian-origin founders in the core group — names like Palo Alto Networks, Bloom Energy, Astera Labs and the AI company Perplexity.

Set against that, the 102 unicorns based in India account for approximately $349 billion, led by Flipkart at $36 billion, Zomato at $30 billion and Groww at $16 billion.

Why America wins

Geography explains most of the gap. Within the overseas unicorn index, 91% — 187 of the 205 companies — are based in the United States. A broader birth-origin analysis in the report, covering founders who left India as children alongside India-based companies, found that 62% of its 323 companies sit in the US, with 200 either started there (178) or relocated there (22).

The pattern is familiar: deep capital pools, mature technology ecosystems and the world's largest enterprise software market make the US the default arena for founders chasing multi-billion-dollar scale. India produces the talent; America, most of the time, provides the runway.

How the numbers were built

The methodology matters. The index took each company's valuation, divided it equally among the founders, and counted the slice attributable to qualifying Indian-origin founders — regardless of their actual shareholding. The $560 billion is therefore an indicative figure, a measure of the value Indian founders helped create rather than what they personally own.

Even with that caveat, the direction is unambiguous, and it echoes earlier findings: the Hurun Global Unicorn Index has previously noted that Indians co-found more offshore unicorns than any other nationality.

What it means for India

Prosus India principal investor Saurav Jain struck an optimistic note, saying Indian founders have the ability to turn technology, ingenuity and deep local insight into businesses that can fundamentally change how people live and work — and that founders no longer need to leave India to build at scale.

That last point is the live question for policymakers and investors. India's domestic startup ecosystem has matured enormously — 102 unicorns is itself a remarkable figure — but the Diaspora Index is a reminder that the country's most valuable entrepreneurial exports still tend to list, raise and scale elsewhere. Closing that gap means competing on capital depth, exit pathways and regulatory ease, not just talent.

What to watch

The index gives investors and policymakers a new baseline to argue over: whether the next decade bends the curve back toward India. Watch for the pace of Indian unicorn IPOs, the growth of domestic late-stage capital, and whether AI-era founders — Perplexity's inclusion hints at the trend — choose to build from Bengaluru or the Bay Area.
